criterion_notes.c1: Examines household sanitation and water service access and use in two urban slums of Hyderabad, India, including ILCS pit latrines, self-financed private toilets, open defecation, absence of underground sewerage, and municipal piped, tanker, tap, and handpump water supply, alongside personal and domestic hygiene practices.
criterion_notes.c2: Fails Criterion 2 under both the narrow 2026-10-13 rule-type reading and the plain wording. Under the narrow 2026-10-13 reading, the study does not examine any rule-type legal, administrative, or regulatory mechanism directly governing service access (no analysis of eligibility screening, administrative burden, documentation or tenure rules, tariffs/cost recovery, official discretion, enforcement, or utility/regulatory structure). Although the methodology notes in passing that Vajpayeenagar is a notified slum and Banjara Colony is a non-notified slum, notification or tenure rules are never analysed as a barrier or determinant of access (both slums received ILCS latrines and municipal water interventions), and remarks on ILCS/VAMBAY construction and municipal neglect reflect generic project delivery and technical design defects (black cotton soil seepage, small latrine dimensions, lack of sewerage). Under the plain wording of Criterion 2, the study likewise fails because it does not empirically examine a legal, administrative, institutional, regulatory, or governance factor as its exposure; instead, it investigates women's perceptions of cleanliness, personal/menstrual hygiene practices, intra-household gender division of cleaning chores, and physical latrine/soil conditions, offering only unanalysed programme background and concluding normative calls for hygiene education and women's participation in programme planning.
criterion_notes.c3: Contains primary empirical qualitative/participatory fieldwork in two urban slums, combining household questionnaires, in-depth guided-checklist interviews across 32 stratified households, focus group discussions with women, adolescent girls, children, and men, and direct observation.
criterion_notes.c4: Reports descriptive/qualitative outcomes relevant to household sanitation and water access and usability, including non-use of overflowing ILCS pit latrines, reliance on open defecation after latrine demolition under housing construction or due to lack of underground drainage, private toilet investment by better-off households, and water availability constraints.
criterion_notes.c5: Population and units of analysis (household and individual residents in two Hyderabad slums, n = 32 in-depth household interviews plus FGDs), exposures examined by the authors (economic/vulnerability category, gender roles, and physical/technical latrine and soil drawbacks), outcomes, and participatory qualitative study design are clearly identifiable, though the exposure is outside review scope.

evidence_quotes.quote: Based on field work in two urban slums of Hyderabad, Andhra Pradesh, this article points out that sanitation implies much more than defecation issues and that it converges on several important aspects of life, such as shame and dignity and personal hygiene.
The study was conducted in two slums of Hyderabad, Vajpayeenagar (a Notified Slum) of Qutbullapur municipality and Banjara Colony (a Non-Notified Slum) of LB Nagar Municipality.

raw_response.exposure: Household socio-economic/vulnerability category, gender norms and intra-household division of cleaning labour, and physical/technical conditions of sanitation facilities (soil suitability, pit latrine design/size, and lack of underground sewerage)
raw_response.outcome: Definitions and daily practices of sanitation and personal/menstrual hygiene, time and gender allocation of domestic cleaning tasks, and household sanitation/water use (use vs non-use of ILCS pit latrines, self-financed private toilet construction, open defecation, and coping with water scarcity)
raw_response.population_and_sample: Residents (poor and vulnerable women, adolescent girls, school-going children, and men) in two urban slums of Hyderabad, Andhra Pradesh (Vajpayeenagar, pop. ~2,413; Banjara Colony, pop. ~2,500); 32 households interviewed in depth (8 across each of 4 economic categories) plus focus group discussions (units of analysis: household and individual)
raw_response.rationale: Exclude under E03 (Wrong exposure). While this empirical participatory study in two Hyderabad slums examines household sanitation and water access/use alongside personal and domestic hygiene practices (satisfying c1, c3, c4, c5, and c6), it does not examine a legal, administrative, institutional, regulatory, or governance factor governing service access under either the narrow 2026-10-13 rule-type reading or the plain wording of Criterion 2. Its empirical analysis centres on local definitions of cleanliness, gendered household cleaning burdens, menstrual and ritual hygiene practices, and physical/technical flaws of ILCS pit latrines (seepage in black cotton soil, small size, and absence of underground sewerage), mentioning slum notification status, government schemes (ILCS, VAMBAY), and municipal neglect only as unanalysed background and generic project-delivery context.
raw_response.study_design: Participatory qualitative field study (individual questionnaires, guided-checklist in-depth household interviews, focus group discussions, and direct observation)
